title: Capstone Part 4 - Testing, Documentation, and Handover
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Capstone Part 4 — Testing, Documentation, and Handover ##### The restore that failed at 3 a.m. A platform had nightly backups. The cron job ran, the dump landed in object storage, and the monitoring said green for fourteen months. Then a bad migration corrupted a table. The on-call engineer downloaded the most recent dump and discovered two things: the `pg_dump` had been running against the *replica* with a stale connection string and had been producing 4 KB files containing only a schema header since a database migration nine months earlier. And nobody knew the restore procedure, because it had never been performed. Recovery took eleven hours of reconstructing state from application logs. The backup existed. The **verified restore** did not. That distinction — between an artefact and a proven capability — runs through everything in Part 4. A test suite nobody runs, a runbook nobody has followed, documentation nobody has read: each is a comfortable illusion until the night it matters. ##### The full test suite in CI Everything from Day 31, now assembled as a gate on the capstone. ```yaml jobs: quality: steps: - run: ruff check . && ruff format --check . && mypy src/ unit: needs: quality steps: - run: pytest tests/unit -q --cov=src --cov-fail-under=80 integration: needs: quality services: postgres: { image: postgres:16-alpine, ... } redis: { image: redis:7-alpine, ... } steps: - run: alembic upgrade head - run: pytest tests/integration -q # real SQL, real queues isolation: # multi-tenancy guarantee needs: integration steps: - run: pytest tests/isolation -q -x # fails the build on any leak e2e: needs: integration steps: - run: pytest tests/e2e -q # VCR cassettes, offline ai-evals: if: contains(github.event.pull_request.changed_files, 'prompts/') steps: - run: python -m evals.run --min-accuracy 0.90 --max-parse-failure 0.02 ``` Three suites are specific to this system and worth calling out. **Isolation tests** query without a tenant filter and assert zero cross-tenant rows — proving RLS is enforcing the boundary rather than your queries. Run them with `-x` so a leak stops the pipeline immediately. **AI eval tests** gate prompt and model changes against a labelled set, converting silent model drift into a failing build. **Idempotency tests** run concurrently — ten threads delivering the same event, asserting exactly one row — because sequential duplicate tests pass even when a race exists. ```python def test_concurrent_duplicate_delivery(engine, signed_event): with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool: list(pool.map(lambda _: post_webhook(*signed_event), range(10))) with engine.connect() as c: assert c.execute(text("SELECT count(*) FROM events")).scalar() == 1 ``` ##### Documentation that works The **Diátaxis** framework separates documentation by what the reader is trying to do, and it prevents the common failure of one long page serving nobody: | Type | Reader's need | Your artefact | |---|---|---| | **Tutorial** | Learning by doing | "Deploy the platform locally in 20 minutes" | | **How-to** | Solving a specific problem | Runbooks: deploy, rollback, restore, replay DLQ | | **Reference** | Looking something up | API spec, workflow catalogue, config variables | | **Explanation** | Understanding why | Architecture doc, ADRs | The structure that follows: ```text docs/ ├── README.md what it is, who it serves, how to start ├── 01-architecture.md C4 diagrams + data model (Part 1) ├── adr/ ADR-001 … ADR-004 ├── tutorials/local-setup.md ├── runbooks/ │ ├── deploy.md │ ├── rollback.md │ ├── restore-from-backup.md │ ├── replay-dead-letters.md │ ├── rotate-credentials.md │ └── incident-response.md ├── reference/ │ ├── api.md generated from OpenAPI │ ├── workflows.md generated from workflow metadata │ └── configuration.md every env var, purpose, default └── CHANGELOG.md ``` Generate what can be generated — the API reference from OpenAPI, the workflow catalogue from workflow metadata — because hand-maintained reference documentation drifts within weeks. ##### Runbooks A runbook is written for someone woken at 3 a.m. who did not build the system. That means: exact commands, expected output, and what to do when it goes wrong. ```markdown # Runbook: Restore from backup **Severity:** critical · **Est. time:** 25 min · **Owner:** platform team **Last verified:** 2026-03-14 by ananya (quarterly drill) ## When to use Data corruption, accidental deletion, or failed migration that `alembic downgrade` cannot repair. ## Before you start - Announce in #incidents. Set the status page to "degraded". - Scale workers to zero so nothing writes during the restore: `kubectl scale deployment/n8n-worker --replicas=0` ## Steps 1. Identify the target backup (list newest first): ```bash aws s3 ls s3://acme-backups/platform/ --recursive | sort | tail -10 ``` Expected: daily `.dump` files ~180–260 MB. **A file under 1 MB is a failed backup — do not use it; choose the previous good one and raise a separate incident for the backup job.** 2. Download and verify integrity: ```bash aws s3 cp s3://acme-backups/platform/2026-03-13.dump /tmp/ pg_restore --list /tmp/2026-03-13.dump | head # must list tables ``` 3. Restore into a scratch database first — never straight over production: ```bash createdb platform_restore pg_restore -d platform_restore --no-owner --jobs=4 /tmp/2026-03-13.dump psql -d platform_restore -c "SELECT count(*) FROM events;" # sanity check ``` 4. Verify row counts are within expectation, then promote: ```bash psql -c "ALTER DATABASE platform RENAME TO platform_corrupt_$(date +%F);" psql -c "ALTER DATABASE platform_restore RENAME TO platform;" ``` 5. Bring the system back: ```bash kubectl scale deployment/n8n-worker --replicas=3 curl -fsS https://automation.acme.in/healthz/ready ``` 6. Replay events received during the outage window: ```bash python -m scripts.replay --since "2026-03-13T00:00:00Z" --source all ``` Safe to run twice: processing is idempotent on `event_id`. ## Verification - [ ] `SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE received_at > ` matches replay count - [ ] Grafana success rate back above 99.5% - [ ] Dead-letter table not growing - [ ] One end-to-end test event processes successfully ## If this fails Escalate to . Do not delete `platform_corrupt_*` — it is evidence. ``` Note what makes this usable: the **failure signal** in step 1 (a small file means the backup itself failed), the **scratch restore** before promotion, the **replay** step that closes the data gap, and an explicit **verification checklist**. The `Last verified` line at the top is the discipline that would have caught the opening story. ##### Backup and disaster recovery Define the two numbers that govern every decision here: - **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)** — acceptable data loss. Nightly dumps give 24 hours; add WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery within minutes. - **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)** — acceptable downtime. Measure it during a drill rather than estimating. What must be backed up: the **database** (dumps plus WAL), the **n8n encryption key** (stored separately — without it, backed-up credentials are unreadable), **workflow definitions** (in Git), **Terraform state**, and **Vault data**. ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail STAMP=$(date +%F) FILE="/tmp/platform-$STAMP.dump" pg_dump "$DATABASE_URL" -Fc -f "$FILE" # VERIFY the dump before shipping it — this is what was missing SIZE=$(stat -c%s "$FILE") if [ "$SIZE" -lt 10000000 ]; then # < 10 MB is suspicious echo "Backup only ${SIZE} bytes — failing loudly" >&2 curl -fsS -X POST "$ALERT_WEBHOOK" -d "{\"text\":\"Backup verification FAILED: ${SIZE} bytes\"}" exit 1 fi pg_restore --list "$FILE" > /dev/null # structural integrity check aws s3 cp "$FILE" "s3://acme-backups/platform/$STAMP.dump" curl -fsS "$HEALTHCHECK_PING_URL" # dead-man's switch: alerts if absent ``` Two safeguards there: **size and integrity verification** so a broken dump fails loudly, and a **dead-man's switch** ping so a backup job that stops running triggers an alert rather than silence. Then run a **quarterly restore drill** into a scratch environment, time it, and update the `Last verified` line. An untested backup is a hypothesis. ##### Versioned release notes ```markdown ## [1.4.0] — 2026-03-14 ### Added - Support-desk source adapter (ADR-004) - Per-tenant AI cost attribution in `usage_events` ### Changed - Worker concurrency default 4 → 8 after load testing (see capacity note) - Confidence threshold for auto-send raised 0.75 → 0.85 ### Fixed - Duplicate invoices when Stripe redelivered `checkout.session.completed` during a deploy (idempotency key now derived from event ID, not timestamp) ### Migration notes - Requires `alembic upgrade head` (adds `usage_events.cost_usd`) - **Backward compatible.** Rollback to 1.3.x is safe; the new column is nullable. ``` The **migration notes** section is the one operators read. State whether rollback is safe, because that is the question during an incident. ##### The handover ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Docs complete] --> B[Pick a fresh reviewer
who did not build it] B --> C[They deploy to a
scratch environment
using docs only] C --> D[They break something
and recover it] D --> E[Log every question
they had to ask you] E --> F{Questions asked?} F -->|yes| G[Each one = a doc gap
→ fix it] G --> C F -->|no| H[Handover complete] ``` The rule that makes this work: **you may not speak during the exercise.** Every question they need to ask is a documentation defect, and the list of questions is the most valuable output of the whole day. A handover checklist worth working through: repository access and branch protection; secrets access and the credential inventory; monitoring dashboards and alert routing with a named owner; the runbook set, each verified; on-call rotation and escalation path; known issues and the deferred-work list; cost ownership and budget alerts; and a scheduled 30-day follow-up. ##### Common pitfalls - **Backups never restored** — the opening story. - **No size or integrity verification**, so a broken dump looks successful. - **No dead-man's switch**, so a backup job that stops running is silent. - **Runbooks written by the person who built it**, assuming context nobody else has. - **Documentation without a `Last verified` date**, so nobody knows if it is current. - **Reference docs maintained by hand** rather than generated. - **Handover as a presentation** instead of an exercise the other person performs. - **Answering questions during the handover test**, hiding the gaps. - **Coverage as the test goal** rather than covering real failure modes. - **No isolation or idempotency tests** in CI for a multi-tenant system. - **Release notes without migration and rollback guidance.** ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: ship the platform's **full test suite in CI** plus **complete documentation** — architecture, runbooks, API reference, backup and restore — then run a **mock handover** where someone else deploys and recovers it. Prioritize the restore runbook, because it is the one most likely to be needed and least likely to have been rehearsed. The mini project is that documentation set, built with Diátaxis structure and with generated reference material so it cannot drift. Add the `Last verified` discipline to every runbook and schedule the next verification date. For the assignment, **do the mock handover: have someone else deploy and recover the platform using only your docs, and fix any gaps**. Log every question they ask, and report the list alongside the fixes. A write-up saying "they asked eleven questions; here they are and here is what I added" is far more credible than one claiming the documentation was complete first time — and the eleven answers are precisely what makes the platform survivable without you. ##### Key takeaways - A backup is not a capability until you have restored from it; verify dump size and integrity, add a dead-man's switch, and drill the restore quarterly. - Gate every change in CI with unit, integration, isolation, idempotency (concurrent) and AI-eval suites — the last three are what a multi-tenant AI platform specifically needs. - Structure documentation by reader intent (Diátaxis) and generate reference material so it cannot drift from the code. - Write runbooks for a stranger at 3 a.m.: exact commands, expected output, failure signals, verification checklist, and a `Last verified` date. - Test the handover by having someone else perform it in silence; every question they ask is a documentation defect worth more than any review.
